revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Wrapping the Time Capsule
revealWordProblem.text: A time capsule box is shaped like a rectangular prism that is 9 in long, 4 in wide, and 5 in tall. You unfold it into a net so you can see all six faces laid flat. How many square inches of wrapping paper are needed to cover the whole box? Explain your reasoning.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Unfolding the box into a net shows 3 pairs of faces. SA = 2(9×4) + 2(9×5) + 2(4×5) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202. You need 202 in² of wrapping paper.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do we find the surface area of a box?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: A box has 3 pairs of matching faces, so add up all 6 faces to get the surface area — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: My box is 8 long, 5 wide, and 3 tall. I unfold it into a net and see 3 pairs of faces.
Top and bottom: each is 8 × 5 = 40, and there are 2 of them, so 2 × 40 = 80.
Front and back: each is 8 × 3 = 24, so 2 × 24 = 48.
Left and right: each is 5 × 3 = 15, so 2 × 15 = 30.
I add all the pairs: 80 + 48 + 30 = 158. The surface area is 158 in².

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Identify each face of the rectangular time capsule box (l = 8 in, w = 5 in, h = 3 in). Find the area of each face pair, then calculate the total surface area. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

onLevel.stem: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its surface area?
onLevel.explanation: A cube has 6 identical faces. Each face: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Total SA = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
choiceFeedback: That's the volume calculation (edge cubed) — surface area needs six face areas added together.
Check the units — a flat surface is measured in square units, not cubic.
Square the edge length for one face's area first, then multiply by the number of faces.
hints: A cube's 6 faces are identical squares, each one 5 cm by 5 cm.
Find the area of one square face, then multiply by 6 — and keep square units (cm²).
One face is 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Now multiply that area by the number of faces, 6.

extending.explanation: A cube net has 6 equal square faces. With each face 4 cm², the surface area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

Check again — did you count the face directly opposite the one you started with?

extending.stem: A time capsule box measures 2 in × 3 in × 4 in. Using its net, you add up all six faces. What is the total surface area?
choiceFeedback: That's the volume calculation — surface area needs the sum of all six face areas instead.

hints: Surface area covers all 6 faces of the 6 × 4 × 2 box — it's not the same as the space inside.

extending.stem: How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
extending.explanation: A rectangular prism has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left, and right.
choiceFeedback: Don't forget the top and bottom — a box has faces all around it, not just the sides.
That's the number of corners (vertices), not the number of flat faces.
That's the number of edges, not the number of flat faces — count the flat surfaces instead.
hints: Picture a cereal box in your hands. Turn it: there's a front, a back, two sides, a top, and a bottom.
Count faces in opposite pairs — every face on a rectangular prism has a matching partner across from it.

extending.stem: Surface area is measured in which type of unit?
extending.explanation: Surface area measures flat surfaces, so it uses square units. Volume uses cubic units.
choiceFeedback: Cubic units measure 3D volume, not a flat surface — surface area needs a different kind of unit.
Linear units only measure length in one direction — surface area covers a flat region, needing two dimensions.
Every measurement needs a unit — think about what kind of unit matches a flat, two-dimensional surface.
hints: Surface area measures the flat covering on the outside of a solid — like wrapping paper.
Flat 2D measurements use square units. Save cubic units for filling space and plain units for length.
Imagine covering one face with 1-inch squares. Each square is 1 in² — that's the kind of unit surface area counts.

workedExample.label: Read
workedExample.work: A time capsule box from the net is l = 6 in, w = 4 in, h = 2 in. Find the surface area.

workedExample.work: SA = 24 + 24 + 12 + 8 + 8 = 76 in² (only one front/back face counted)

extending.correctWork: The student only counted one 12 in² front/back face. The net shows both a front AND a back, so both 12 in² faces must be added. Correct: SA = 24 + 24 + 12 + 12 + 8 + 8 = 88 in².

The front face (12 in²) has a matching back face (12 in²). Add both.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Surface Area Using Nets is finding the area of only one face from each of the 3 matching pairs and forgetting to double it, instead of counting all 6 faces. For a box that is 9 in × 4 in × 5 in, a student might add just one face from each pair: (9×4) + (9×5) + (4×5) = 36 + 45 + 20 = 101 in², but the net actually has two of each face, so the correct total is 2(36) + 2(45) + 2(20) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202 in² — exactly double. Before you submit, ask: 'Did I count both matching faces in each pair, or only one from each pair?'
